lesson.title: Code That Explains Itself: Writing for Humans, Not Just the Interpreter
lesson.summary: Code readability is the practice of writing programs so that other people, and your own future self, can understand them quickly, relying mainly on meaningful variable names and well-placed comments, since Python runs confusing code exactly as fast as clear code.
lesson.body:
Python's interpreter does not care whether a variable is named x or radius, and it does not read comments at all; both compile down to the exact same instructions once the program runs. Readability exists entirely for the benefit of the humans who read, use, and maintain the code, not for the machine executing it. This is easy to forget while focused on simply getting a program to work, but it becomes obvious the first time you reopen your own code weeks later and cannot remember what it does.

Compare two lines that compute the exact same value using the exact same operator precedence rules: x = 3.14159 * r ** 2 versus area = 3.14159 * radius ** 2. Both square the radius and multiply by an approximation of pi, and both run identically fast. But the second line communicates its purpose instantly, while the first forces a reader to guess what x and r represent. This connects directly to Variable Naming Rules, which govern what names are legal, since both x and area are legal identifiers; readability is the separate, further choice of which legal name actually communicates intent.

Comments extend the same idea to explaining reasoning that a name alone cannot capture. A comment begins with a # symbol, and everything after it on that line is ignored completely by the interpreter, existing purely for a human reader. A useful comment explains why, not what: raw_score = int(input("Enter test score: ")) followed by curved_score = raw_score + 5, with a comment reading # apply the department's standard 5-point curve above that second line, tells a reader something the code alone cannot, namely the reason 5 is being added. A comment like # add 5 to raw_score, restating a line that already says exactly that, adds nothing.

Trace a before-and-after example with identical behavior. The unclear version reads t = int(input("Enter test score: ")); t2 = t + 5; print(t2). The readable version reads raw_score = int(input("Enter test score: ")); curved_score = raw_score + 5  # apply 5-point curve; print(curved_score). Given the same typed input, 90, both versions perform the identical augmented-assignment-style addition and print 95. Neither version is faster or more correct than the other in any way Python can measure; the only difference is how quickly a person can understand what each line is for.

This matters because real code is read far more often than it is written: by a teammate reviewing it, by a grader evaluating it, or by the original author returning to it after enough time has passed to forget the details. Every idea in this chapter, expressions, statements, operators, assignment, string handling, is only as useful in practice as the names and comments wrapped around it, since clear code is what lets all of those correct computations actually be trusted, checked, and built upon by someone other than the interpreter.
